analysis.one_liner: Extends and raises federal price supports for wheat, barley, oats, wool, mohair, sugar beets, and honey.
analysis.headline: The bill, introduced with zero cosponsors by a single senator, was referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the day it arrived and never received a hearing, a markup, or a vote before Congress ended.
analysis.plain_summary: Senator Conrad Burns of Montana proposed locking in federal price supports for wheat, barley, oats, wool, mohair, sugar beets, honey, and several oilseed crops through the 1995 crop year, with guaranteed minimum prices that would rise every year. The government would pay growers the difference whenever the market price fell below those floors. The bill also extended the conservation reserve program, ordered studies of Canadian grain imports, and required noxious weed control on federal land. It never got a hearing or a vote.
analysis.who_benefits: Producers of the supported commodities: wheat, barley, and oat growers (with minimum target prices rising each year to $4.40, $2.60, and $1.60 per bushel respectively by 1995), wool and mohair ranchers, sugar beet growers, honey producers (supported at 55 cents per pound), and growers of flax, safflower, and canola, who would have gained a brand-new subsidy. Program participants would also get advance deficiency payments of 30 to 50 percent of their projected payment before harvest. Barley growers who owed refunds on 1988-89 advance payments would get those bills recalculated downward, with interest paid if the government repaid late. Montana producers — Burns's home-state wheat, barley, wool, and honey growers — were the clearest intended constituency, and landowners would have gained new options to enroll wetlands, shelterbelts, and windbreaks in the conservation reserve program.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Commodity crop, wool, sugar, honey producers

how_it_helps.text: Extends the wool and mohair price support program, the sugar beet support program, and the honey program (at a fixed 55 cents per pound) through the 1995 crop, so producers of these commodities keep a government-guaranteed price regardless of what the market pays.

Sets rising minimum target prices for wheat ($4.08 per bushel in 1991 up to $4.40 in 1995), barley ($2.41 to $2.60), and oats ($1.48 to $1.60), with the government making up the gap between those floors and the market price through deficiency payments.
Creates a new subsidy for oilseed growers — flax, safflower, and rapeseed (canola) — with loans and graduated payments previously unavailable to those crops.

Requires the Secretary of Agriculture to make advance deficiency payments covering 30 to 50 percent of the projected payment available to wheat and feed grain producers before harvest, improving their cash flow during the growing season.

Recalculates the advance deficiency payment refunds owed by feed barley producers for the 1988 and 1989 crops, reducing what they owe to reflect malting barley prices, and repays with interest any excess already collected by the government.

Extends the conservation reserve program — which pays landowners to take erosion-prone land out of crops — through 1995 and makes wetlands, shelterbelts, and windbreaks eligible for enrollment, capping total enrollment at 40 million acres.
Keeps payment limitations and foreign-person ineligibility rules in force through 1995 and applies them to the new oilseed payments, capping how much any one operation can collect.

Directs a joint Agriculture-Interior program to control noxious weeds such as leafy spurge and knapweed on all federal lands, and declares brucellosis eradication a national emergency funded through the Commodity Credit Corporation.

analysis.who_pays: Taxpayers, through the Commodity Credit Corporation, would fund the deficiency payments, loan operations, land diversion payments, storage payments, conservation payments, and brucellosis program — with the guaranteed price floors set to climb each year through 1995. Consumers would bear part of the cost indirectly, since price supports for sugar beets and other storable commodities hold market prices above world levels, which shows up in food prices. When the government pays growers the difference between a legislated floor and the world price, the difference comes from the Treasury, not from buyers.

drawbacks.text: The bill would have committed the Treasury to rising price floors every year through 1995 and to deficiency payments covering the gap whenever markets fell below those floors, making federal farm spending larger and less responsive to actual prices and demand.

Guaranteed minimum prices for wool, mohair, honey, and sugar beets are paid regardless of demand — the mechanism rewards producing for the support price rather than for customers, which is why these programs had repeatedly generated surpluses and large payments concentrated on a relatively small number of operations.

Land diversion payments would have paid growers to take wheat, barley, and oat acreage out of production (capped at 40 million acres combined with the conservation reserve), so taxpayers would fund idled land while consumers paid above-market prices for supported crops.

The bill had no cosponsors and was written largely around the commodities and problems of one state — including removing Montana from a regional spearmint marketing order and ordering studies of Canadian durum wheat and alfalfa imports — so it offered no broader coalition a reason to advance it.

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The bill had some genuinely public-spirited pieces — extending the conservation reserve with wetlands and shelterbelt eligibility, noxious weed control on federal land, and keeping payment limits and foreign-ownership restrictions in force. But its core was a five-year extension and escalation of price supports for a fixed list of commodities, with floors rising each year and new subsidies added for oilseeds. The cost of guaranteeing prices above world levels lands on taxpayers and food consumers, while the gains concentrate on program-crop producers and the largest operations. The design offered no offsetting spending discipline, and the absence of even one cosponsor suggests it was written more for its sponsor's state than for a national coalition.

outcome.mechanism: It was introduced with no cosponsors, referred to the Senate Agriculture Committee the same day, never taken up by that committee, and died when the 101st Congress ended.

narrative.text: Senator Conrad Burns introduced the Agricultural Recovery Act of 1990 in the Senate on March 30, 1990.
The bill was read twice and referred to the Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry the same day it was introduced.
No senator from either party signed on as a cosponsor.
The committee took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — and the bill's action history ends with the referral; it expired when the Congress ended on January 3, 1991.

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Taxpayers and food consumers came out ahead in the narrow sense that the guaranteed price floors, new oilseed subsidies, and advance payments in the bill never took effect. Program-crop producers gained nothing from this bill either, leaving the existing farm programs unchanged by it.

for.name: Sen. Conrad Burns
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill on March 30, 1990, and could not attract a single cosponsor from either party.

against.name: Senate Committee on Agriculture, Nutrition, and Forestry (chair Patrick Leahy)
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and never reported it out — no hearing, no markup, no vote; the action record ends there.

sides.party_line_note: No vote was ever held, so no partisan split can be measured; the bill had one Republican sponsor, zero cosponsors of either party, and died in a committee led by a Democrat.

industries.note: The bill's largest titles would have guaranteed these growers minimum prices rising every year through 1995, with deficiency payments and 30-50 percent advances covering the gap between the floor and the market. The cost of that guarantee falls on taxpayers, and the floors push production beyond what the market alone would support.

Extending the National Wool Act supports through 1995 continues a program that pays ranchers a guaranteed price for wool and mohair regardless of demand, with payments historically concentrated on a small number of large operations.
Extended sugar beet price supports keep the domestic sugar price above the world price, which benefits growers and processors at the direct expense of food consumers and manufacturers who buy sugar.
The bill locks in honey price supports at 55 cents per pound through 1995; the honey program's guarantee has historically rewarded production aimed at the support price rather than the market.
These crops would have become newly eligible for federal loans and graduated payments, creating a fresh class of subsidy recipients financed by the Commodity Credit Corporation.

industries.industry: Spearmint oil producers in the Far West marketing order
industries.note: Removing Montana from the regional spearmint marketing order frees Montana growers from its handling restrictions while leaving the remaining order states' producers subject to them, slightly shifting the burden within a small regulated market.
Declaring brucellosis eradication a national emergency and funding it through the Commodity Credit Corporation would have sped up removal of a cattle disease that restricts herd movement and trade.
